title: Executive Summary
description: Bottom line for Rental increase SF, with every finding linked to an official source.

sections.title: FOREFRONT - Is the "inform the Rent Board" law state or local? (local)

rows.label: The direct answer
rows.value: LOCAL. The duty to report a rent-controlled unit to the SF Rent Board and hold a Rent Increase License comes from the San Francisco Administrative Code (Chapter 37, Sec. 37.15), added by Ordinance No. 265-20 effective January 18, 2021. It is not a California state statute and not a federal rule.
rows.notes: This is the answer to the state-vs-local question, placed first. Full layer-by-layer table on the Local Law page (LAW-01 to LAW-08).

rows.label: Where the '2023' date comes from
rows.value: 2023 is the year the LOCAL duty became operative for condominiums and buildings with 1-9 residential units (March 1, 2023). It is not the year a state law passed. Buildings with 10 or more units began reporting July 1, 2022; the ordinance itself dates from January 18, 2021. A two-unit building is in the 1-9 unit group.
rows.notes: Rent Board Rule 13.14 states the same two dates and tests the increase's effective date, not the date of service.

rows.label: What the real 2023 state law was
rows.value: SB 567 (Chapter 290, Statutes of 2023) amended the statewide Tenant Protection Act - just-cause eviction rules and enforcement of the state 5%-plus-CPI / 10% rent cap - and became operative April 1, 2024. It creates no rent-board reporting duty.
rows.notes: Negative finding from the chaptered bill text.

rows.label: Why the state cap is not this owner's ceiling
rows.value: Civil Code 1947.12(d)(3) excludes housing under a stricter local rent control ordinance, and SF.gov states AB 1482 does not apply to units under the SF Rent Ordinance limits. The local 1.6% for 3/1/26-2/28/27 governs covered SF units.
rows.notes: State 8.8% is not an alternative the owner may elect.

rows.label: So what must the owner actually do?
rows.value: Report into the Rent Board Housing Inventory through the Rent Board Portal (free, due March 1 each year), which generates the Rent Increase License; confirm the license is on file on the increase's effective date; then serve the compliant written notice. There is no separate licence application form.
rows.notes: Step-by-step page: PRC-01 to PRC-12. The Rent Board Fee is a separate obligation (FEE page).

sections.title: FOREFRONT - Rent Board & Rent Increase License: individual owner

rows.label: Does an individual (non-corporate) owner still need the license?
rows.value: Yes - SF.gov states 'a landlord must get a rent increase license before imposing annual allowable and/or banked rent increases'; no individual-owner exception is stated on the official pages re-fetched 2026-11-07
rows.notes: Ownership form (individual vs corporation) is not listed as an exemption. Do not rely on being a small/individual owner.

rows.label: Small buildings (1-9 units) timing
rows.value: Requirement effective July 1, 2022; March 1, 2023 for condominiums and buildings with 1-9 residential units
rows.notes: A small individual-owned building is therefore covered now (2026).

rows.label: Step 1 - Report to the Rent Board (Housing Inventory)
rows.value: All owners of residential property are required to report through the Rent Board Portal; reporting is free, online 24/7, due March 1 every year
rows.notes: This reporting is how you 'inform the Rent Board'. Information submitted is public; submit under penalty of perjury.

rows.label: Step 2 - License is generated
rows.value: Property owners who report a unit as tenant-occupied receive a rent increase license; it is automatically generated for non-owner-occupied units
rows.notes: The license does not need to be included with the rent increase notice to tenants.

rows.label: Step 3 - License must be current BEFORE the increase takes effect
rows.value: A landlord must have a current rent increase license on file with the Rent Board before any annual or banked rent increase can go into effect; a notice is not enforceable without a license on the effective date
rows.notes: Legal test: the license must be current on the effective date. Recommended conservative order: report -> confirm license -> serve notice -> effective date. See flag F25 on consequence wording.

rows.label: Late reporting
rows.value: You can still submit and receive a license after the March 1 deadline; the Rent Board does not assess monetary penalties for late filing - but the increase notice is not enforceable without a license on the effective date
rows.notes: Late filing does not cure a notice whose effective date passed without a license; get legal advice on any already-served notice.

rows.label: Step 4 - Only then notify tenants
rows.value: 30-day written notice (90-day if >10% alone/combined in same year; +5 days if mailed) stating dollar amount, percentage and effective date, using the rate in effect on the increase date
rows.notes: License first, tenant notice second. License alone does not satisfy state/local notice law; you must still comply with all other rent increase laws.

rows.label: Can tenants check?
rows.value: Tenants can search the Rent Board Portal to see if their landlord is up to date with their rent increase license; if you miss the deadline the Rent Board may notify tenants you are not in compliance
rows.notes: Assume tenants and free tenant-side legal services can and will check this before paying an increase.

rows.label: This case: license / Housing Inventory status
rows.notes: Owner-supplied intake does not confirm Housing Inventory reporting or a current license for either unit; blank and flagged. No increase should be treated as effective until this is confirmed.

rows.label: Rule 13.14 quoted verbatim (re-read 2026-11-13)
rows.value: "Any rent increase under Ordinance Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2) purporting to be effective while the landlord is unlicensed shall render the entire rent increase null and void; provided, however, that the effective date of the rent increase, not the date of service, shall be used to determine whether or not the increase conforms with the provisions of this section. Nothing in this Regulation shall affect a landlord's banking rights or the ability to accumulate otherwise lawful rent increases that were found to be null and void. This section shall apply to all rent increases that are effective on or after July 1, 2022, except that with respect to condominium units and buildings with less than ten residential units, this section shall only apply to rent increases that are effective on or after March 1, 2023."
rows.notes: Read on 2026-11-13. This is the strongest wording in the record and it narrows flag F25: the softer 'may be null and void' / 'will not be enforceable' phrasing on the tenant-facing pages does not soften the rule text, and an owner's banking rights survive a void increase.

rows.label: What an individual owner is exposed to if the licence is not on file on the effective date
rows.value: Under Sec. 37.15(e) the licence is "temporarily suspended during the period of the landlord's noncompliance" and "a tenant shall not be obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the period of suspension"; separately, SF.gov states there is no monetary penalty from the Rent Board for reporting late. So the exposure is money back to the tenant for the suspended months, not a City fine for the late report itself.
rows.notes: A tenant who paid an increase while the owner was unlicensed can petition for the difference; there is no time limit on a tenant petition. Nothing here exempts an individual owner.

rows.label: Rent Increase License
rows.value: Current license required before annual/banked increase takes effect
rows.notes: Unlicensed increase may be null/void.

rows.label: Notice
rows.value: 30-day written; 90-day if >10%; +5 days if mailed; dollar amount, percentage, effective date
rows.notes: Use rate in effect on increase date.

rows.label: Banked increases
rows.value: Only if >=24 full months without any increase; add percentages, do not compound/prorate
rows.notes: No banked amount inferred for this case.

rows.label: Roommate / additional occupant
rows.value: Cannot charge extra rent merely because a new/additional roommate moved in
rows.notes: No market-rate reset inferred.

rows.label: Unit 1 vacancy-decontrol issue
rows.notes: Continuing occupant legal status and last-original-occupant facts unverified.

rows.label: Corporate practice
rows.value: IRT Q4 2025 same-store renewal 2.9%, new -3.7%, blended 0.8%; Invitation Homes 2025 renewal 4.6%, new -0.8%
rows.notes: Portfolio-level, not SF-specific and not a legal benchmark.

rows.label: Individual practice
rows.value: June 2024: 23 landlord petitions/154 units; 73 tenant petitions; 89 eviction notices
rows.notes: Narrow formal-petition evidence only.

rows.label: Conservative approach
rows.value: Identical, neutral, license-and-notice-compliant <=1.6% policy on each eligible unit; or less
rows.notes: Compliance checklist capable of tenant-lawyer review; no approval or guarantee.

rows.label: One unit or both
rows.notes: No official source requires both; document neutral eligibility reasons if only one is raised.

rows.label: Pending banked-increase legislation
rows.value: File 261020 is proposed, not enacted; it could limit combined banked and capital-improvement increases to 10% per year.
rows.notes: If enacted as proposed, it would apply to banked notices and capital-improvement petitions from September 15, 2026; check status before relying on a banked calculation. F46.
